analysis.one_liner: Forces hospitals, labs, imaging providers, and insurers to publish real prices in plain, comparable formats.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: after being referred to the Senate health committee in December 2023, it sat there until the Congress ended in January 2025.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would strengthen federal price transparency rules that already exist on paper. Hospitals, labs, imaging centers, and surgery centers would have to publish their real prices — including the discounted cash price and the rates they actually negotiate with each insurer — in a standard, free, machine-readable format, and could be fined up to $10 million a day for repeated refusal. Insurers would have to give patients an online tool showing what a specific procedure would cost them out of pocket, and employers buying health coverage would gain the right to see the claims data and fees that third-party administrators and pharmacy benefit managers currently keep hidden. The bill was introduced in December 2023 and never advanced out of committee.
analysis.who_benefits: Patients shopping for scheduled care (lab tests, imaging, surgery) gain published cash prices and insurer-specific rates before treatment, and cash-paying patients get a legally binding discounted price. Workers whose employers self-insure health benefits — covering a large share of Americans with job-based coverage — gain visibility into the fees and claims data that third-party administrators and pharmacy benefit managers currently withhold. Insurers must provide real-time out-of-pocket cost estimates and remain liable if estimates are wrong.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Patients and employers paying for health care

how_it_helps.text: Requires hospitals to publish their actual prices — list charges, discounted cash prices, and the rates they negotiated with each insurer — in a standard free online format, instead of leaving patients to discover costs only after treatment.
Requires hospitals to honor their published discounted cash price as payment in full for any patient paying cash, and to link to a plain-language explanation of their charity care policies.
Extends the same price disclosure rules to clinical labs, imaging providers, and surgery centers, which are outside the existing hospital rule.

Requires insurers to offer a real-time online tool that tells a patient their expected out-of-pocket cost, deductible progress, and any prior-authorization requirements before they get care, and holds patients harmless if the estimate is wrong.

Gives employers and other health plan sponsors the legal right to see their own claims data and contract terms from third-party administrators and pharmacy benefit managers, and voids secrecy ('gag') clauses that block plan audits — with $10,000-per-day penalties for violations.

Raises penalties for hospitals that repeatedly refuse to comply, up to $10 million, and requires annual government audits of insurer price files — addressing the weak enforcement that limited earlier transparency rules.

analysis.who_pays: Hospitals, clinical labs, imaging providers, and surgery centers bear compliance costs and, for hospitals, fines up to $10 million for persistent refusal to disclose. Insurers must publish detailed negotiated rates and build real-time cost tools. Third-party administrators and pharmacy benefit managers face $10,000-a-day penalties for withholding data and can no longer enforce secrecy clauses.

drawbacks.text: Compliance is a real burden: hospitals, labs, imaging providers, and surgery centers would have to publish hundreds of prices monthly in machine-readable form, and smaller facilities could struggle with the cost of maintaining those systems.

Transparency alone does not set prices. Publishing rates does not by itself lower what patients or employers pay, and some health economists argue that publishing negotiated rates can even push some hospitals' rates upward, toward the higher end of the disclosed range.

The bill relies on the Secretary of Health and Human Services to write detailed format and penalty rules, so its practical effect would depend heavily on how faithfully future administrations enforce it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The benefits are real but depend entirely on enforcement and follow-through: disclosure alone does not set prices, and patients still have to navigate confusing bills even with the data available. The costs are compliance burdens on hospitals and labs, plus a risk that publicizing negotiated rates could, in a worst case, give large systems leverage to demand higher rates in some markets. On balance the transparency provisions address a genuine, well-documented gap — rules that required price disclosure but were weakly enforced — and the costs are modest relative to the scale of U.S. health spending.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee, which never acted on it, so the bill expired when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Sen. Mike Braun introduced the bill on December 14, 2023, with Sens. Sanders, Smith, and Hickenlooper as original cosponsors.
The Senate's only action was to read the bill twice and refer it to the Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed.
The bill drew 12 cosponsors from both parties, including independents aligned with Democrats, but never progressed.
The 118th Congress ended January 3, 2025, and all bills not enacted by then died.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Hospitals, insurers, and pharmacy middlemen avoided enforceable price disclosure and the threat of daily fines for hiding negotiated rates.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Hospitals, insurers, and middlemen who avoided disclosure

sides.party_line_note: The bill was bipartisan from introduction — its cosponsors split roughly evenly between Republicans (4 of 49) and Democrats plus an Independent (8 of 52) — and there is no record of organized opposition; it simply stalled in committee without a vote.

industries.note: The bill would force hospitals to publish negotiated rates, honor discounted cash prices, and face fines up to $10 million for willful noncompliance — a direct threat to the opaque, contract-by-contract pricing that keeps hospital revenue high. Hospitals that already follow the rules would face little new burden.

Insurers would have to publish negotiated rates for every service monthly, build consumer cost-estimation tools, and submit to government audits of their data files. Better price information weakens their ability to quietly steer patients to higher-cost providers.

industries.industry: Pharmacy benefit managers and third-party administrators
industries.note: The bill voids contract clauses that hide fees, rebates, and claims data from the employers who hire these middlemen, and adds $10,000-a-day penalties — squarely aimed at middlemen profits built on undisclosed spreads.

Large employers gain access to the claims and pricing data they currently cannot see, which could help them cut health costs — though big hospital systems they negotiate with lose the information advantage.
